name: Polyglot Butler
one_liner: Speak to the G1 in your own language: one Gemma 4 E2B turn hears the clip and sees the camera frame together, emits a native tool call, and the robot fetches a can and hands it to you; no ASR, no second vision model, no cloud, about 1.5 s from the end of your sentence to the robot moving.
story: My mother speaks Mandarin and no English. Every 'smart' device in her house wants an English wake word, a cloud account and a phone. This robot needs none of that. (Presenter turns to a volunteer.) Say anything to it in your language. (Volunteer, in Spanish: '¿Me traes la lata roja?') What just happened took one model and one turn: the microphone clip and the camera frame went into Gemma 4 E2B together; it understood Spanish, saw a red can and a green can on the table, and emitted a single tool call, serve(item='red can', language='es'), that our code turned into motion. No Whisper, no separate vision model, no planner, no server anywhere; the Wi-Fi radio is off, you can check on the screen. The handover is the one physical act that makes the point: the robot faces the person who spoke, walks to them, and lets go when it sees their hand on the can. Everything on the slide was measured on the Jetson inside the robot this week: a voice turn with an image in about a second and a half, every perception step under a second, because we run E2B with thinking off at 70 image tokens and let the model's own tool grammar do the structuring. The same loop answers in your language, waves when asked, and says 'I don't see a blue can' instead of inventing one. One two-billion-parameter Gemma in a 35-kilogram body, hearing and seeing for a person who was never going to learn English.
demo_script: BENCH (repeats per judge group, ~3 min; robot standing in FSM 500 inside a taped 2x2 m foam square, teammate 1.5 m away holding the R3 remote with thumbs on L2+B; bench screen shows the live 480x336 frame, the raw Gemma request/response stream with ms, and `ip -br link` proving all radios down). 0:00 Presenter: 'Pick any language, press the button on this mic, ask it for a drink or ask what it sees.' Judge takes the wireless push-to-talk mic. 0:20 Judge speaks (e.g. French: 'Tu vois quoi sur la table?'); LED blue while listening, green when VAD cuts the clip (1.2 s silence); screen shows the audio+image request and ~1.2 s later Gemma's one-sentence reply in French, spoken by the Piper fr voice on the USB speaker. 0:50 Judge asks for one ('Donne-moi la verte'); screen shows serve(item='green can', language='fr') with latency and client-side validation; robot says 'Tout de suite'. 1:00-1:40 Execution with overlays: box_2d on 'green can' (~0.8 s) maps to a table slot, the recorded arm_sdk reach trajectory for that slot plays, BrainCo closes to 0.7, lift to chest, robot says 'Voilà', extends toward the judge (ShakeHand-style), opens when the 'Is a hand holding the can?' yes/no gate fires (3 s timer fallback). 1:40 Participatory #2: another judge says 'high five' or '挥挥手' → gesture(name) → ExecuteAction(18 or 26). 2:10 Failure-recovery, always shown: presenter asks for an absent item ('la lata azul') → gate says no → 'No veo ninguna lata azul; tengo roja y verde.' If a pick failed earlier, the in-hand gate says no and the robot says 'I missed, trying again' and re-runs; judges see the retry. 2:40 Presenter shows the Orin latency table and the one-page architecture, offers the mic for one more question. Between groups the robot is Damped on its stand if the gap exceeds 10 min; battery swap at lunch. STAGE (2:30, top-six demo; 3x3 m clear floor; spotter with remote). 0:00-0:15 opening (the mother line). 0:15-0:35 pre-asked audience volunteer who speaks Spanish or Mandarin asks for the red can; the projected screen shows the tool call with ms. 0:35-1:20 robot picks the red can, faces the speaker (box_2d 'person' → bearing), walks ~2 m in 1-s Move pulses, stops at 0.8 m by depth, extends, releases on the hand gate; the volunteer holds the can up. 1:20-1:45 a second volunteer in another language asks it to wave and what it sees; reply in that language. 1:45-2:05 honest failure: 'bring the blue can' → 'I don't see one.' 2:05-2:30 slide: measured Orin latencies, the radios-off proof, the rehearsal success table (n, misses per stage), 'one model, one turn'. Backup video on the laptop in case of a hardware fault.
gemma_role: Gemma 4 E2B IT (unsloth QAT UD-Q4_K_XL GGUF + the mmproj that carries the gemma4a audio encoder, both already cached) as one llama-server process on PC2 (CUDA arch 87, --jinja, -np 1 --cache-ram 0 -c 4096 --swa-full, thinking off, greedy), serving two request shapes on one warm cached prefix. (1) Voice turn: [system: cached persona + tools] [user: 480x336 head-camera JPEG, then the 16 kHz mono VAD clip as input_audio, then one line 'Answer in the speaker's language or call a tool'] → native tool call serve(item, language) | gesture(name ∈ wave, high_five, heart, clap, handshake) | stop(), or a one-sentence reply in the speaker's language. (2) Perception loop: image then a direct question: box_2d with assistant prefill for 'green can' / 'person' (slot and bearing), yes/no gates ('Is a hand holding the can?', 'Is there a blue can?'), one-word answers. All arguments validated client-side (the native grammar does not enforce enums; the template orders arguments alphabetically). E4B (Google QAT Q4_0 + mmproj, cached) is loaded only if the day-2 language test shows E2B failing a demo language (E4B is 15-25% better at speech, 1.6x slower). Why Gemma is essential: audio and image enter the same turn, so there is no ASR and no second VLM; the reply language comes from the model's native speech understanding; the trained six-token tool format plus llama.cpp's native tool grammar gives structured actions without a wrapper; and the measured 70-image-token sub-second perception path is the only reason a 35-kg humanoid closes the loop in real time on a 16 GB Orin. Swap it for any other open model and you need Whisper + a VLM + a function-calling shim, three models in the memory we use for one. Thinking stays off everywhere and the slide says why (brief thinking was 63% accurate at 2.1-2.6 s on the Mac).
litert_role: LiteRT-LM is the audited second engine, not decoration: the identical Gemma 4 E2B .litertlm bundle (litert-community, 2.58 GB, vision+audio loaded on demand) runs under litert-lm-api on the Orin CPU as the hot standby for the voice turn (Engine(backend=CPU, audio_backend=CPU, vision_backend=CPU, max_vision_tokens_per_image=70), Content.AudioFile, Python-function tools, LLGuidance ResponseFormat.json for the arguments), switchable from the bench UI. Day 1 we also try --backend=gpu with the prebuilt/linux_arm64 LD_LIBRARY_PATH workaround from issue #2570. If GPU runs at model-card class (~24 tok/s decode, sub-second TTFT), the voice turn moves to LiteRT-LM permanently and the bench slide shows both engines side by side, which puts Best Use of LiteRT in play. If only CPU runs (expect 3-6 s per voice turn), it stays the standby, the slide shows the first public Orin NX LiteRT-LM audio numbers, and we do not claim the LiteRT award on that basis. No Pi or Pixel side-brain in this concept: a second Gemma that only hears would duplicate the robot's own hearing and judges would read it as padding.
architecture: Devices: everything runs on G1 PC2 (Orin NX 16 GB, JetPack 6.2); the MacBook is only the bench display (a browser page served by PC2 over our own USB Wi-Fi AP at 10.42.0.1; venue Wi-Fi and Tailscale off). Processes on PC2: (a) llama-server with E2B + mmproj (~4.5 GB GPU incl. 4096 KV). (b) butler.py state machine (Python, unitree_sdk2py over DDS on eth0 192.168.123.164): mic thread (ALSA capture from the UAC wireless receiver, Silero VAD ONNX on CPU, 1.2 s end-of-speech, 15 s cap, USB button override), camera thread (D435i color 640x480 via pyrealsense2 after `mscli stopservice video_hub_pc4`, resized to 480x336 JPEG q85), skill layer (LocoClient.Move/SetVelocity/StopMove in FSM 500, G1ArmActionClient.ExecuteAction ids 17/18/20/26/27 and 99 to release, arm_sdk LowCmd at 50 Hz replaying recorded joint trajectories with the weight ramp while the built-in controller balances, BrainCo rt/brainco/right/cmd six positions 0..1 at 100 Hz), safety (depth/LiDAR min-range stop at 0.8 m, odometry rt/odommodestate distance cap 3 m per approach, remote timeout halts). (c) Piper TTS (en/es/fr/de/zh ONNX voices on CPU, ~0.3-0.6 s per sentence) → USB speaker via ALSA; Unitree AudioClient.LedControl for the LED states and AudioClient.PlayStream/TtsMaker as the speaker fallback; the onboard mic stays off so the factory assistant never wakes. (d) LiteRT-LM standby engine, lazy-loaded. Data flow: VAD clip + latest frame → /v1/chat/completions (cache_prompt, tools, max_tokens 48) → validation → state machine → skills; each skill step asks the one perception question it needs on a fresh frame. Expected Orin latencies (to be measured day 2; Mac numbers in LATENCY_RESULTS.md): voice turn with image, 4-s clip (~100 audio + 70 image + ~150 text tokens, 15-token tool call) 1.0-1.6 s; box_2d 0.65-0.9 s; yes/no gate 0.3-0.45 s; TTS 0.4 s; pick-and-handover motion 25-40 s. MTP drafter enabled only if the Orin A/B shows a gain on tool-call decode (net loss on the Mac). Memory budget ~9-10 GB of 16 (llama-server 4.5, LiteRT-LM standby ~3 when loaded, Piper 0.3, RealSense 0.5, Unitree services ~2).

name: The Robot That Remembers
one_liner: A humanoid with an on-device episodic memory: all day it embeds what it sees and hears with EmbeddingGemma 2 on LiteRT-LM; ask it in any language 'where did you last see my keys?' and Gemma 4 recalls the moment, verifies it live, answers with time and place, and walks back to point at the spot; nothing is stored or sent off the robot.
story: Everyone in this room has lost their keys this month. My father, who has early memory loss, loses them every day, and the only product for him is a tracker tag with a cloud account. This robot has been standing here watching this bench for two hours. Every few seconds it captured a frame and a few words, and EmbeddingGemma 2, the two-week-old multimodal embedding model, running on LiteRT-LM on the Jetson in its chest, turned them into vectors. No image ever left the robot and no faces are stored, only places and things. (To a judge.) Earlier you put your badge somewhere while it watched. Ask it where, in any language. (Judge, in German: 'Wo ist mein Ausweis?') One Gemma 4 turn heard that in German and called recall('badge'). EmbeddingGemma 2 found three candidate moments; Gemma 4 looked at the best one again and confirmed it really shows a badge, so it does not guess. It answers in German, 'fourteen minutes ago, on the shelf behind you', and now it turns, walks back to the spot it remembers, and points. Two Gemma models, 740 million and 2 billion parameters, both on the robot, both offline: memory, hearing, seeing and checking. It also remembers what people asked; ask what the last judge wanted. Everything on the slide was measured on this robot this week, and the retrieval is honest: it says 'I haven't seen it' when the memory has nothing.
demo_script: BENCH (memory capture runs continuously from 10:15; robot standing in its taped square, spotter on the remote; the bench screen shows the live frame, the memory timeline of thumbnails with Gemma captions, the request stream with ms, and the radios-off panel). 0:00 Presenter: 'It has been watching this bench all day. Put something of yours anywhere it can see, then let me show you the architecture for a minute.' 0:20 Judge places a badge/keys/phone case; the screen shows the new frame being captioned by Gemma 4 ('a lanyard badge on the grey shelf', ~0.5 s) and embedded by EmbeddingGemma 2 (CPU, ~1 s, a tick on the timeline). 0:40-1:30 Presenter walks through the one-page architecture while the robot keeps embedding; privacy line: no face embeddings, memory wiped at 17:00. 1:30 Participatory: the judge takes the push-to-talk mic and asks in any language 'Where did I put my badge?'; LED blue then green; screen shows recall(query='badge', kind='object') with ms (~1.2 s), three candidate thumbnails with similarity, Gemma 4's yes/no verification on the top frame (~0.4 s), then the answer spoken in the judge's language with elapsed time and place. 2:00 Robot turns toward the stored bearing (Move(0,0,vyaw) pulses), re-detects the badge live (box_2d overlay), raises its arm toward it (arm_sdk pointing pose) and says 'there'; if the bench is too crowded to walk, it points from where it stands. 2:30 Second query: 'What did the last person ask you?' → recall(kind='conversation') → it repeats the previous request. 2:50 Failure-recovery, always shown: ask for something it never saw ('my umbrella'): every candidate fails the verification gate → 'I haven't seen an umbrella today.' Or an item that moved: top-1 is the old spot, the gate fails on the live frame, the robot says 'it was there at 12:40 but it is not there now' and shows the second candidate. 3:20 Latency slide (Orin numbers), the litert-lm serve log window (/v1/embeddings calls), hand the mic to the next judge. STAGE (2:30; the robot walked the stage 20 minutes earlier while a teammate placed four props; the projector shows that walk on the memory timeline). 0:00-0:20 opening (the father line). 0:20-0:45 a volunteer asks in their language for one prop ('¿dónde está la taza amarilla?'); tool call on screen, three candidates, verification tick, spoken answer in Spanish with elapsed time and place. 0:45-1:30 the robot turns and walks ~3 m to the stored odometry pose (Move pulses, depth stop), re-detects the mug (box_2d overlay projected), points and says 'aquí'. 1:30-1:50 a second volunteer: 'what did she ask you?' → the robot repeats it in English. 1:50-2:10 honest failure: 'where is the drone?' → 'I haven't seen one.' 2:10-2:30 slide: measured numbers, EmbeddingGemma 2 per-image embedding time on LiteRT-LM CPU, llama.cpp CUDA for Gemma 4 E2B, memory size (N frames), the privacy line.
gemma_role: Two Gemma models on PC2. (1) Gemma 4 E2B IT on llama-server (CUDA, thinking off, greedy, cached prefix) with three jobs: the captioner (every 2-3 s: 480x336 image + 'Describe the objects and where they are, in eight words' → ~12-token caption, ~0.5 s, stored with pose and time); the voice turn (image + input_audio clip + question → native tool call recall(query, kind ∈ object|conversation) or a short reply written in the speaker's language); and the verifier/grounder (retrieved frame + 'Is there a <query> in this image? yes/no' at ~0.35 s, then on the live frame box_2d of <query> with assistant prefill at ~0.8 s to get the pointing bearing). (2) EmbeddingGemma 2 (740M, litert-community bundle, 485 MB) under LiteRT-LM on the Orin CPU: image(+caption) embeddings for every memory frame, text+audio embeddings for every spoken request, text embeddings for queries; cosine top-k in numpy. Why Gemma is essential: EmbeddingGemma 2 is the only open text+image+audio embedding model that ships for an edge runtime, so camera and microphone memories live in one index; Gemma 4 hears the query natively in the speaker's language (no ASR) and turns it into a tool call; and the recall-then-verify loop depends on E2B's sub-second yes/no and box_2d answers on 70-token frames. A 'retrieve and trust' system built on any other model would either hallucinate or take seconds per check. Thinking is off everywhere and the slide says so as a deliberate choice.
litert_role: Genuinely in the loop and visible: `litert-lm serve` (0.18.0, port 9379) hosts EmbeddingGemma 2 and every memory write and every query hits its POST /v1/embeddings (if the server does not accept image/audio parts, the same model runs in-process via litert-lm-api Engine(backend=CPU, vision_backend=CPU, audio_backend=CPU), still LiteRT-LM). CPU is the officially supported LiteRT-LM path on Jetson, so this placement is credible; EmbeddingGemma 2 landed in LiteRT-LM two weeks ago and /v1/embeddings is new in 0.18.0, so a LiteRT judge sees their newest feature doing what it was built for (the Gallery's media search) inside a humanoid's loop. Day 1 we also try the GPU (WebGPU) path with the prebuilt/linux_arm64 LD_LIBRARY_PATH workaround; if it works, the Gemma 4 E2B captioner moves onto LiteRT-LM GPU as a second visible job, measured side by side with llama.cpp. Gemma 4 E2B's sub-second loop stays on llama.cpp CUDA and the slide says so plainly.
architecture: Devices: G1 PC2 (Orin NX 16 GB) runs everything; the MacBook is only the bench display over our own AP. Processes: (a) llama-server E2B + mmproj (~4.5 GB GPU). (b) litert-lm serve with EmbeddingGemma 2 (CPU, 6 threads, ~1-1.5 GB RSS). (c) memory.py: capture thread (D435i color at 2 Hz → 480x336 JPEG for the models, 640x480 JPEG on the USB SSD for the timeline), caption request to llama-server (0.5 s, serialized behind the voice loop on the single slot), embed request (CPU, expect 0.5-2 s per image on the Orin, measured day 1; frames queue if slower), index = numpy float32 matrix + JSON rows {t, pose (x, y, yaw) from rt/odommodestate, caption, jpeg path, kind}; conversation memory: every VAD clip's Gemma tool-argument text plus its EmbeddingGemma 2 text+audio embedding. (d) recall.py state machine: voice turn → validation → embed query → top-3 by cosine within kind → Gemma verify top frame (yes/no; on failure try the next) → answer text written by Gemma in the query language with elapsed time and the caption's place → Piper TTS → USB speaker; then navigate: heading to the stored pose, Move(0,0,vyaw) pulses then Move(vx) pulses with odometry feedback, stop at 0.8 m or on the depth/LiDAR guard; re-detect with box_2d on the live frame → bearing → arm_sdk pointing pose (shoulder pitch/yaw from bearing, 50 Hz LowCmd with weight ramp) with preset 23 right-arm-up plus waist yaw as the fallback. (e) Safety as in Polyglot Butler (spotter, L2+B, 3 m cap, depth stop). Expected Orin latencies: caption 0.4-0.6 s; image embed 0.5-2 s on CPU in the background; voice turn with image 1.0-1.6 s; cosine top-k < 5 ms over 5,000 rows; verify 0.3-0.45 s; box_2d 0.65-0.9 s; TTS 0.4 s; walk-back 10-25 s. Memory ~9-10 GB total; the captioner yields the llama-server slot whenever a voice turn starts.

name: Show Me Once
one_liner: A judge demonstrates a two-step tabletop chore while talking; Gemma 4 watches the keyframes and hears the narration in one turn, thinks briefly, writes a schema-constrained JSON plan, and the G1 repeats the chore with its own arm, checking each step with sub-second Gemma detection.
story: Google's brief for today says 'a robot that learns a chore from watching you once'. Here is the honest six-day version of that sentence. (A volunteer steps up to the table.) Show it something: slide the red cup next to the blue box, then push the green can to the edge, and just say what you are doing as you do it. The robot's camera took one frame a second; we kept the six frames where your hands slowed down and sent them, with your twenty seconds of narration, into a single Gemma 4 turn with thinking on. (The screen shows the reasoning, then a JSON plan.) Gemma wrote that plan under a JSON schema, so it cannot name an action the robot does not have. Now watch it work: for each step it looks again, finds the cup with Gemma's box detection in under a second, pushes it, looks again, and only moves on when Gemma confirms the cup is next to the box. Everything you see is one two-billion-parameter model on the Jetson in the robot's chest: it heard, it watched, it reasoned, and now it is checking its own work. If a push misses, it looks and pushes again; you will probably see that happen, because we do not hide it. No teleoperation, no cloud, no training run: a person who has never written code taught a humanoid a chore in twenty seconds, and the latencies on the slide are from this robot, this week.
demo_script: BENCH (~3 min per group; robot in locked stand FSM 500 at a 90-cm table inside a taped foam square, spotter on the remote; bench screen shows the camera, the selected keyframes, Gemma's thinking stream, the JSON plan and the request stream with ms). 0:00 Presenter explains in 20 s; the judge picks two of four objects and a two-step arrangement from a card (allowed relations: next to, left of, right of, in front of, behind, to the edge). 0:20 Participatory: the judge demonstrates while narrating into the push-to-talk mic (≤ 25 s; LED blue = watching; 1 fps frames). 0:50 Robot says 'let me think about what I saw'; screen shows six keyframes chosen by motion energy, the single request (6 images x 70 tokens + the narration clip + the schema), thinking tokens streaming (budget 256), then the plan [{action: push, object: red cup, relation: next_to, target: blue box}, {action: push, object: green can, relation: to_edge}] in ~6-10 s. The judge may correct it by voice ('no, left of the box') → a second turn on the same KV. 1:05 The judge puts the objects back (we do not claim reset). Step 1: box_2d on red cup and blue box (140-280 tokens, ~1 s), table-plane mapping, arm_sdk IK push 10-15 cm with a closed fist, re-detect, up to four pushes; yes/no gate 'Is the red cup next to the blue box?' → step 2. 2:30 Failure-recovery (happens naturally; otherwise the presenter nudges the cup mid-way): the gate says no, the robot says 'not yet' and pushes again. 2:50 Latency slide plus the plan-accuracy table from 30 recorded demos (n, per relation). Judges with only 60 s get the 'replay the last plan' button. STAGE (2:30). 0:00-0:15 opening. 0:15-0:40 a volunteer demonstrates a two-step chore, narrated. 0:40-0:55 thinking and the plan on the projector. 0:55-2:05 the robot executes both steps with live detection overlays. 2:05-2:20 a visible retry. 2:20-2:30 the numbers slide (plan accuracy, per-step latency, radios off). Backup video on the laptop.
gemma_role: Gemma 4 E2B IT on llama-server (CUDA) in two modes on the same weights. Watch-and-plan turn: thinking ON with a 256-400 token budget; 4-8 keyframes as 480x336 images at 70 tokens each (Gemma 4's documented 1 fps video mode), the narration as input_audio ≤ 25 s, output constrained to the plan schema (steps[≤3] of {action ∈ push|point, object, relation ∈ 6 enums, target}) via llama.cpp json_schema (no tools in this request, so the grammar is allowed) or the native tool call set_plan(steps) if that proves more reliable. Execution loop: thinking OFF, greedy: box_2d of named objects with assistant prefill at 140-280 image tokens on a cropped table view (the 70-token budget misses objects in clutter), yes/no relation gates, and 'which object moved?' one-word checks. E4B (Google QAT Q4_0 + mmproj, cached) is the candidate for the plan turn only if E2B scores < 70% on the recorded demo set; it reasons better and 1.6x slower is fine for one turn, with both models loaded (~8 GB GPU) or E4B serving both roles at 0.6-1.4 s per perception step. Why Gemma is essential: video-as-frames and audio in one context with a thinking toggle is a Gemma 4 capability; box_2d is a trained output; the trained tool/JSON formats make the plan executable without parsing heuristics; and E2B's speed makes closed-loop visual checking affordable on an Orin NX. The same pipeline with a text-only or vision-only model needs an ASR, a detector and a planner.
litert_role: GPU-conditional, and we say so. The watch-and-plan turn is latency-tolerant (the robot says 'let me think'), which makes it the right home for LiteRT-LM: Engine(backend=GPU, max_vision_tokens_per_image=70) with ThinkingConfig(budget) and ResponseFormat.json(schema) under LLGuidance gives schema-enforced plans out of the box, and the Python API accepts several images plus Content.AudioFile in one turn. Day-1 spike: GPU via the prebuilt/linux_arm64 LD_LIBRARY_PATH workaround; if it runs, the plan turn is served by LiteRT-LM and shown on the bench next to the llama.cpp execution loop, measured. If only CPU works, a 6-image + audio turn would take tens of seconds (ARM CPU vision encoding is seconds per image), so LiteRT-LM is not in the loop, we do not claim the LiteRT award, and there is no Pi or Pixel padding.
architecture: Devices: G1 PC2 runs everything; the MacBook is the bench display over our own AP. Processes: (a) llama-server E2B (plus E4B if chosen) on CUDA. (b) watch.py: 1 fps capture from the D435i during the demonstration (LED blue), motion-energy keyframe picker (frame differencing inside the table ROI; 4-8 troughs/peaks), VAD-trimmed narration WAV (≤ 25 s, 16 kHz mono), one plan request → JSON validated against the enums → optional voice-correction turn on the same KV. (c) do.py executor: per step, box_2d on the table crop (140-280 tokens) → table-plane mapping (D435i depth via pyrealsense2 after `mscli stopservice video_hub_pc4`, or a one-time homography from four taped marks at the fixed table height) → push waypoint behind the object → xr_teleoperate's pinocchio IK (robot_arm_ik.py, G1_23 arm config) solves the wrist target → arm_sdk LowCmd at 50 Hz with the weight ramp (kp 60 / kd 1.5) while FSM 500 balances, hand held as a closed fist (BrainCo 0.9) for pushing; re-detect after each 10-15 cm push; relation gate (yes/no) ends the step. (d) Piper TTS for spoken status. (e) Safety: arm workspace box, velocity limits in the LowCmd ramp, table-edge stop, LowStand only if reach needs it, spotter on L2+B. Expected Orin latencies: plan turn (6 x 70 image tokens + ~500 audio tokens + schema, ~300 thinking + 60 output tokens) 6-12 s with E2B, 10-18 s with E4B; box_2d at 280 tokens 1.0-1.4 s; gate 0.35 s; each push 3-4 s; a two-step chore ≈ 60-90 s end to end. Memory 6-10 GB.
hardware_to_buy: Wireless UAC mic for the narration, two brands (DJI Mic Mini ~$90; Hollyland Lark M2S or Rode Wireless Micro ~$100-150)
Powered USB speaker (~$50), powered USB-C hub (~$30), USB push-to-talk button (~$25)
Counter-height (90 cm) folding table (~$60-90) with a non-slip mat and taped reference marks (~$20)
High-contrast props with weighted bases: red cup, blue box, green can, yellow bowl (~$30)
2x2 m foam mat and floor tape (~$60); travel router/AP (~$60); portable HDMI monitor (~$150)
Optional second USB webcam on a mini-tripod above the table for the keyframe timeline on screen (~$70); phone tripod for the backup video (~$20)
Spare G1 battery if not already owned (dealer price). Total ≈ $600-800 without the battery
prize_targets: Track 2 Physical AI, IoT & Robotics 1st-3rd: it is the sentence on Google's own event page, on a humanoid, honestly scoped, with a participatory teacher
Best Use of LiteRT: only if the GPU spike moves the plan turn onto LiteRT-LM; otherwise not claimed
No hardware awards (no partner silicon in the loop)
why_it_wins: Highest ceiling of the three: the organizers wrote 'learns a chore from watching you once' on the event page, and this is the first humanoid in the room that does it with a single on-device Gemma turn that watches and listens at once, thinks visibly, and then checks its own work with sub-second detection. The judge is the teacher, the retry is a feature rather than a hidden failure, and the plan-accuracy table shows we measured instead of cherry-picked.
build_plan: Oct 18 (Sat, D-6). A (owner, runtime): on the Mac, record 10 phone demos of two-step chores with narration, extract 1-fps frames, build the keyframe picker and the plan request (multi-image + input_audio + json_schema, thinking on) and score E2B vs E4B on the 10 demos (the decisive spike; no robot needed). B (robot): study xr_teleoperate robot_arm_ik.py and g1_arm5_sdk_dds_example.py, design the push primitive and the workspace limits. C (voice+UI): order hardware, the 90-cm table and props; mic/VAD/TTS setup. D (story/logistics): story, organizers' questions, request a counter-height table and floor space at the venue, Arm Create ticket.

Oct 19 (Sun, D-5). One person at Arm Create with a phone video. Robot online: A builds llama.cpp CUDA on PC2, times the multi-image + audio turn and sweeps the thinking budget. B checks FSM 500 locomotion (only needed to approach the table), replays an arm_sdk trajectory while standing (suspended first), tries IK static targets at table height and measures the reach envelope at 90 cm vs LowStand. C gets the D435i working from PC2 (stop video_hub_pc4; pyrealsense2 or a librealsense Jetson build), depth + color aligned, table plane. D runs the LiteRT-LM GPU spike on PC2.

Oct 20 (Mon, D-4). A builds the execution loop (box_2d at 280 tokens on the table crop → plane mapping → waypoint). B runs the push primitive on the real table with a spotter: 20 pushes, displacement error, balance logs. C builds narration capture, the keyframe timeline UI and the plan-correction voice turn. D records 20 more demos for the accuracy table and builds the bench UI.

Oct 21 (Tue, D-3). Integrate watch → plan → execute → gate; relation gates; failure branches (missed push, object out of reach → ask the judge to move it closer, plan rejected by schema → re-ask); safety limits and the table-edge stop.

Oct 22 (Wed, D-2). 20 end-to-end trials with four testers as teachers → success table per stage (keyframes, plan, step 1, step 2); fix the top two causes; record the backup video; measure battery runtime.
Oct 23 (Thu, D-1). Code freeze at noon; dress rehearsal with outsiders; pack the table, props, mat, mic, router, monitor, batteries; print.

Oct 24 (Sat, event). 07:30 load. 10:00 setup: tape the table marks, re-check the homography, smoke test one chore. Judge rounds with Damp on the stand between rounds. 15:00 stage prep: re-mark the stage table.
first_48h_spikes: Plan accuracy offline on the Mac, no robot: 10-20 narrated phone demos → keyframes + audio → Gemma 4 E2B and E4B, thinking on vs off, 70 vs 140 tokens per frame; pass: ≥ 70% exact plans with E2B or ≥ 80% with E4B, else the concept degrades to narrate-and-point
Push primitive on the real robot: IK to a point on a 90-cm table, 10-15 cm push with a fist, 20 trials, displacement error and balance (rt/lowstate) in FSM 500; LowStand if reach is short
D435i depth/color from PC2 under JetPack 6.2 and the box_2d → table-plane point error (pass: < 3 cm) vs the homography fallback
Multi-image + audio single turn on PC2 llama.cpp CUDA: 6 images + a 20-s clip + json_schema + thinking budget 256 → wall time and looping check (pass: < 12 s, valid JSON 10/10)
LiteRT-LM GPU on PC2 with the LD_LIBRARY_PATH workaround (decides the LiteRT claim)
Detection in clutter: box_2d accuracy on the table set at 70/140/280 tokens and on a crop; pick the budget
risks: Plan accuracy from a 2B model (SeeDo's open baselines were near zero without narration; our narration carries most of the plan) → narrate-and-point degrade
Arm reach and IK at table height with 5-DoF arms and no torso pitch; a 90-cm table and LowStand mitigate; table contact can trip the balance controller
Pushing instead of grasping limits chores to sliding relations; say so on the slide
Multi-image + audio is the most exotic llama.cpp path (looping, the 30-s cap, memory) → spike 4 and the two-turn fallback
Thinking on costs 6-12 s per plan; acceptable once, hidden by 'let me think'
D435i under JetPack 6 needs a source build → homography fallback at a fixed table height
Fall risk while reaching near a table edge with BrainCo hands fitted → foam mat, spotter, workspace limits
Bench throughput: each group needs ~3 min; keep a 'replay the last plan' button for judges with 60 s
Gemma audio on the Orin unverified (as in Polyglot Butler)
fallback: If the push primitive is unreliable by Oct 21, the robot still watches, listens and plans, then narrates the plan back and points at each object in order with box_2d-grounded arm pointing ('narrate and point'), which keeps the Gemma-native core intact. If the plan turn is too slow or inaccurate with E2B, E4B takes the plan turn and E2B the loop. If multi-image + audio fails on the Orin, the narration goes in as an audio-only turn followed by the frames on the same KV. The irreducible demo is 'teach it by showing and telling; it tells you what it learned and points', still unique in the room.
angle: Gemma-native purist: in all three concepts one or two Gemma models are the entire cognitive loop on the G1's own Orin NX, and each concept is built around things only Gemma 4 can do (speech straight into the model with no ASR, image and audio in the same turn, the trained tool-call/JSON formats, box_2d detection, the thinking toggle, sub-second E2B at 70 image tokens, EmbeddingGemma 2 on LiteRT-LM). The fast perception loop stays on llama.cpp CUDA because that is the path we have measured; LiteRT-LM is placed only where a judge can point at it doing real work (EmbeddingGemma 2 memory; or the GPU-conditional slow turn), and otherwise we say 'none' rather than pad. Every demo puts measured Orin latencies, a success-rate table with n, a radios-off proof and a visible failure-recovery on the screen, and nothing not working on Oct 23 ships on Oct 24.

name: Polyglot Porter
one_liner: A G1 lobby concierge that hears a guest in their own language through Gemma 4's native audio, turns to face them, reads the real signage with its own eyes to give grounded directions, greets with the right gesture, and hands over water or a key card from its own hip tray, entirely offline on the robot's Jetson.
story: It is 11 pm at an airport hotel. Our judge has just landed from Madrid, the desk is unstaffed, and the only one in the lobby is a humanoid. She says, in Spanish, 'Perdón, ¿dónde están los ascensores?' The light on the robot's chest turns blue while she speaks, then green: 'Los ascensores. Un momento.' It turns to face her, looks at the lobby sign, and says 'A su izquierda, pasando la cafetería,' raising its right arm toward the corridor. She asks for water; the robot reaches to the tray on its hip, lifts a bottle, holds it out until her hand touches it, and lets go. She thanks it; it offers a handshake and says 'Buenas noches.' Thirty seconds later a second guest asks in English where the restroom is and gets the same service. Then the presenter turns to the room: nothing you just saw left this robot. One Gemma 4 E2B on the 16 GB Jetson inside it heard the Spanish, decided what she wanted, read the sign and chose the gesture and the item; EmbeddingGemma 2 looked up the house knowledge; the factory cloud assistant is off and the Wi-Fi is our own access point. Speech to action takes about a second, the sign is read in under half a second, and here is our success table from 60 rehearsal runs, including the ones it got wrong and how it recovered. A concierge that never sleeps, speaks every guest's language, and keeps everything it hears inside the building.
demo_script: BENCH LOOP (about 6 min per judge group; robot standing in FSM 500 on a taped 1x1 m square, spotter holding the R3 remote with L2+B, hip tray with two 330 ml bottles and a key-card sleeve, A3 'lobby sign' with icons and arrows on an easel 1.5 m away, laptop beside the robot showing the live log). 0:00 Idle: LED breathing white; a 1 Hz vision loop ('Is a person facing me within two meters? yes/no', 0.3-0.45 s each) notices the judge; robot plays ExecuteAction 26 (high wave) and says, in English then Spanish, 'I'm the porter. Tell me what you need, in any language.' 0:20 PARTICIPATORY: the judge speaks (default far-field ReSpeaker XVF3800 on the chest; a clip-on wireless lavalier or the big push-to-talk button on the chest if the room is loud). LED blue while VAD records (max 8 s), cyan during the Gemma turn (about 1 s). The tool call understood(kind, language) comes back; the robot echoes the request from a pre-written table in the detected language ('Directions to the elevator, got it') and LED goes green. A 1.5 s grace window follows: saying 'no' or raising a palm cancels. 0:40 Grounded directions: one 480x336 frame of the sign, one-word question 'On this sign, does the arrow next to the elevator icon point left, right, or straight?' (0.3-0.45 s); the robot turns that way (Move(0,0,+-0.6) 1 s pulses), raises the arm (ExecuteAction 23), speaks the line in the judge's language. 1:30 Handover: judge asks for water; understood(water, es); recorded rt/arm_sdk trajectory to the hip holster, BrainCo right hand closes to 0.7, lift, present at chest height; 2 Hz vision 'Is a human hand holding the bottle? yes/no'; the hand opens on yes or when the finger state readback shows a pull; arm retracts; action 99. 2:30 VISIBLE FAILURE RECOVERY (trigger scripted, behaviour real): a teammate plays 75 dB lobby noise from a phone while the judge asks again. If the call returns kind=unsure or language=other, LED amber and the robot says 'This lobby is louder than a jet bridge. Was that the restroom or the elevator?' and takes a one-word yes/no answer or a thumbs-up (vision). If it simply misheard, 'no' inside the grace window triggers a shrug (ExecuteAction 15 briefly, then 99) and 'My mistake. Once more?' 3:30 Second judge in English or Mandarin (only languages that passed the Oct 20 validation); farewell handshake (27) or high five (18) chosen by the tool call. 4:30 The judge reads the log screen: audio ms, tool JSON, vision answer, LED state, running success counter; we hand them the one-page numbers sheet. STAGE (2.5 min): presenter tells the story while a judge volunteer plays the guest: one validated language of their choice, one direction question, one handover, one deliberately noisy repeat with the amber ask-back; the robot takes two steps toward the volunteer before the handover only if the Oct 19 FSM 500 test passed; final slide: latency table and the 60-run success table; backup video ready on the laptop.
gemma_role: Gemma 4 E2B IT QAT (unsloth UD-Q4_K_XL plus mmproj-BF16, the files already on the Mac, no new downloads) on PC2 through a CUDA arch-87 llama.cpp build from a post-June commit: llama-server --jinja -ngl 99 -np 1 -c 4096 --swa-full --cache-ram 0, thinking off (chat_template_kwargs.enable_thinking=false), greedy (temperature 0, top_k 1), cache_prompt true. Three request types, each a single direct question, sequencing done in code: (1) AUDIO TURN: cached system prefix (~120 tokens) plus tool JSON (~150 tokens), a short instruction, then the 16 kHz mono WAV as an input_audio part placed last; tools=[understood(kind: enum[directions, water, keycard, greeting, question, repeat, cancel, unsure], language: enum[en, es, fr, de, zh, ja, ko, other])], max_tokens 32, two arguments only (alphabetical order kind, language matches the template's sorting). The one tool call is intent plus language ID; no STT anywhere. (2) VISION TURN: 480x336 JPEG before the text, one-word answers (yes/no, left/right/straight, left/center/right), max_tokens 4; this is the measured 222 ms Mac path, projected 0.3-0.45 s on the Orin. (3) ANSWER TURN, only for kind=question: audio plus the top-3 house-knowledge entries as text, free reply in the guest's language, max_tokens 48, streamed sentence by sentence into Piper. E4B is held in reserve only if the Oct 20 language set shows E2B too weak in a chosen non-English language (E4B speech is 15-25% better but 1.6x slower). Enum values are validated client-side because the native tool grammar does not enforce them. Why Gemma is essential rather than a wrapper: the demo lives on native audio-in with language identification, native function calling and 70-token vision from one 2B-effective model that fits beside the robot stack in 16 GB; replacing it means Whisper plus a language-ID model plus a detector plus a text LLM, more RAM, more latency, and no single-model story. Audio-plus-image in one turn is an optimization we test but do not depend on (known looping failure mode).
litert_role: In the loop in two places, neither on the fast path. (a) EmbeddingGemma 2 (released Oct 6; text, image and audio embeddings) served by litert-lm serve (/v1/embeddings, CPU backend, port 9379) on PC2: a ~60-entry hotel/terminal knowledge base (gates, hours, amenities, directions) is embedded once at boot; the transcript E2B produces for a kind=question utterance is embedded and the top-3 entries are injected into the answer turn. Multilingual embeddings let a Spanish question hit an English fact. Expected tens of ms per query on the Orin CPU (unmeasured; day-one spike). (b) Optional, only if a fourth teammate owns it end to end: a Raspberry Pi 5 16 GB 'desk badge' (USB mic plus 7-inch display) running Gemma 4 E2B through the LiteRT-LM Python API (Engine(backend='cpu', audio_backend='cpu', vision_backend='cpu'), tools=[page_porter]), the same stack as Google's Reachy Mini showcase, taking short intents at the desk and paging the robot over our AP; that is a second LiteRT-LM entry point and the Raspberry Pi award. LiteRT-LM GPU on the Orin (prebuilt linux_arm64 LD_LIBRARY_PATH workaround) is tested on day one; if it runs, the slow answer turn moves to it and goes on the slide, otherwise llama.cpp stays and we say so.
architecture: Devices: PC2 Orin NX 16 GB (everything live), MacBook (dev/eval only, not in the loop on the day), owner's MT7612U USB AP (10.42.0.1) for the log screen and the optional Pi badge, R3 remote in the spotter's hand. Processes on PC2: llama-server (CUDA, E2B, :8080); litert-lm serve (EmbeddingGemma 2, :9379); ears.py (arecord -D hw:XVF3800 -r 16000 -f S16_LE -c 1, energy VAD with 600 ms end-of-utterance, clips capped at 8 s, direction of arrival from xvf_host AEC_AZIMUTH_VALUES, speech accepted only from the front +-60 degrees unless PTT or lavalier); eyes.py (D435i colour via pyrealsense2 after mscli stopservice video_hub_pc4, or a chest USB webcam, resized to 480x336 JPEG q85 in ~15 ms); conductor.py (state machine IDLE -> LISTEN -> UNDERSTAND -> CONFIRM 1.5 s -> ACT -> DONE; owns LED colours through AudioClient.LedControl at >=200 ms spacing: white breathing idle, blue listening, cyan thinking, green understood, amber ask-back, magenta cancel; timeouts and cancel paths); voice.py (Piper aarch64 binary with en/es/fr/de/zh voices, 16 kHz int16 output -> AudioClient.PlayStream in 50 ms chunks on the onboard 3 W speaker, or aplay to a USB speaker for the hall; TtsMaker kept only if it passes the WAN-unplugged test); body.py (LocoClient FSM 500 Move pulses, G1ArmActionClient.ExecuteAction ids 26/27/18/23/15/99, rt/arm_sdk LowCmd publisher at 50 Hz with weight at index 29 for the recorded tray trajectory after ServiceSwitch('g1_arm_example', 0), rt/brainco/right/cmd six positions 0..1 and /state readback, rt/lowstate mode_machine check). The robot-side package lives outside the stdlib-only harness repo and depends on unitree_sdk2py; the harness bench scripts are reused for Orin latency tables. Data flow: mic -> WAV -> llama-server tool call -> conductor -> echo line plus LED -> camera frame -> llama-server one word -> body -> speech. Expected Orin latencies (projections until measured): audio turn 0.8-1.5 s for a 3-5 s clip (Orin Nano Super community report 0.37-0.56 s TTFT; decode ~27 ms/token x 15); one-word vision 0.3-0.45 s; echo audible within 1.5 s of the guest stopping; free answer first syllable about 2 s; turn-in-place 1 s per 30 degrees; handover motion 6-8 s. Memory budget: E2B ~3 GB plus mmproj ~1 GB plus KV, EmbeddingGemma ~1 GB RSS, Piper <0.2 GB, robot services; target under 9 GB measured with tegrastats over 30 min.

prize_targets: Track 2 Physical AI first ($7.5k plus trophy): a humanoid that hears, sees, decides and acts live at the bench, all local, with a success table and a visible recovery

Best Use of LiteRT ($7.5k pool): EmbeddingGemma 2 through litert-lm serve as the house-knowledge memory, plus Gemma 4 E2B on LiteRT-LM on the Pi badge if built; stated honestly as the slow layer beside llama.cpp
Best Use of Raspberry Pi (5x Pi 5) only if the desk badge ships

why_it_wins: It is the Figure-01 shape judges remember (speak, robot shows it heard and saw within about a second, one unmistakable physical act) built from primitives we already have, so reliability is high. It uses the three Gemma-4-specific features the Gemma team is showcasing right now (native audio in, function calling, low-latency vision) and the two-week-old EmbeddingGemma 2, with measured numbers on the slide. The multilingual moment makes every judge a protagonist in their own language, the ask-back and shrug make errors part of the charm, and the airport/hotel setting has an obvious customer (co-host Vitaly Bulatov 'helps companies hire robots'). Everything verifiably runs on the device in front of them: own AP, factory assistant off, log on screen.

name: Lantern
one_liner: A G1 sighted guide for a blind traveller: it narrates what it sees in plain speech, offers a breakaway guide strap, walks the person a few meters to the counter or a free seat while Gemma 4 and the lidar call out obstacles, and places a bottle into their hand, all offline, with an optional Pixel 11 narrator running Gemma 4 on the Tensor TPU through LiteRT-LM.
story: Airports are the hardest places to be blind. The meet-and-assist cart is late, every sign is visual, the gate just changed, and asking strangers gets old by the third time. Our judge puts on a blindfold and becomes that traveller. 'I'm Lantern. I can see the room for you. Where do you want to go?' she hears, from a voice that turns toward her as she speaks. 'The counter,' she says. 'The counter is ahead and to your left, about four meters. Two people are queuing. There is a free chair on your right if you'd rather sit.' She asks for the counter. 'Take the strap at my left hand and say ready.' They walk, slowly. 'Three steps. Someone stepped in front of us, let's wait. Clear, going on.' 'We're at the counter; the agent is on your right.' Water? 'Water, in your right hand, ready?' and the bottle is placed, not dropped, into her palm. A handshake, and 'Have a good flight.' Then the presenter: this robot has no cloud and no operator. One Gemma 4 E2B on the Jetson inside it understood her words, looked at the room every half second, and chose every sentence; the lidar is its white cane; every spatial claim it made came from a measured answer, never from a guess. We walked at a quarter meter per second with a spotter and a breakaway strap because a 35 kg humanoid earns trust slowly. Here are the numbers from 40 guided walks.
demo_script: BENCH (about 6 min per group; no walking in the crowd; robot standing in FSM 500 on a taped square, spotter on the remote, a folding chair and a 'COUNTER' sign placed 2 m away, bottles on the hip tray, log screen). 0:00 The judge closes their eyes or takes the blindfold; a teammate explains the strap is only used on stage. 0:15 PARTICIPATORY: the judge says 'What's around me?' (XVF3800 default, lavalier or chest push-to-talk if loud). LED blue, then cyan; the robot turns to face the voice (DOA azimuth to a yaw pulse, then a vision check 'Is a person in the center third? yes/no'); the audio tool returns guide_request(describe, en); one-sentence scene description (max_tokens 40, about 1.5 s to first syllable): 'A chair on your right, a counter ahead on the left, three people behind you.' 1:00 'Is there a free seat?' -> one-word 'left/center/right/none' from the frame -> 'Yes, on your right, two steps.' 1:45 Optional Pixel narrator: the judge holds up a printed boarding pass; the Pixel 11 (Gemma 4 E2B on the Tensor TPU via LiteRT-LM) reads the gate and time aloud offline; the robot says nothing during it. 2:30 Handover: 'Can I have water?' -> guide_request(water) -> tray trajectory -> 'Water, right hand, ready?' -> the robot waits for 'ready' (one-word audio) or a hand-on-bottle vision yes, then opens. 3:30 VISIBLE RECOVERY: a teammate steps between the robot and the counter; the lidar sector guard trips and the vision 'Is the counter visible? yes/no' goes no; the robot says 'Someone is in front of me and I can't see the counter. One moment.' LED amber; the teammate moves; 'Clear. The counter is ahead-left again.' 4:30 The judge asks anything else in a validated language; the log screen shows the per-question latencies and the safety guard state. STAGE (3 min): a 3 m taped lane, a volunteer judge with the blindfold holds the 40 cm breakaway strap on the robot's left hand; 'ready'; the robot walks at 0.25 m/s narrating, stops when a teammate places a box in the lane ('An obstacle, about one step ahead; let's wait'), continues when it is removed, announces arrival at the counter 1 m from the sign, hands over the bottle, handshake. The presenter talks over the walk; the final slide shows walk success, stop distance, narration latency; backup video ready.
gemma_role: Gemma 4 E2B (same files and llama-server flags as the harness: CUDA arch 87, --jinja -ngl 99 -np 1 -c 4096 --swa-full --cache-ram 0, thinking off, greedy, cached prefix) is the only perception and language model on the robot. Continuous perception loop while guiding, about 2 Hz, each a one-word question after a 480x336 frame (max_tokens 4, 0.3-0.45 s projected on the Orin): 'Where is the counter: left/center/right/none', 'Is a free chair visible: left/center/right/none', 'Is a person standing within two steps ahead? yes/no' (the lidar guard is the real safety; Gemma adds the semantics for the narration). On demand: 'Describe what is in front of the robot in one short sentence for a blind person; name objects and people, do not give directions' (max_tokens 40, about 1.1 s decode plus 0.3 s prefill on the Orin); every direction word in the spoken output comes from a one-word class answer or the lidar, never from the free sentence, and the conductor strips direction words from free text (non-hallucinatory design). Audio turn: input_audio last, tools=[guide_request(goal: enum[counter, seat, restroom, exit, describe, water, stop, repeat, unsure], language: enum[en, es, fr, de, zh, ja, other])], max_tokens 32. Handover check: 'Is a human hand touching the bottle? yes/no' at 2 Hz. Optional Pixel narrator: Gemma 4 E2B gemma-4-E2B-it_Google_Tensor_G6.litertlm through LiteRT-LM Kotlin in a fork of litert-samples sample_app_tpu (TPU -> GPU -> CPU fallback), prompts 'Read this aloud' and 'What is in front of me, one sentence', Android TextToSpeech offline voice, only 'take me to X' intents forwarded to PC2 over our AP. Why Gemma is essential: a guide needs grounded answers from fresh frames several times a second, speech understanding in the traveller's language, and one-sentence descriptions, from one model that fits beside the lidar, camera and robot services in 16 GB; a detector gives boxes, not 'a free chair', and a text LLM cannot see.

TPU tokens per second stay off the slides (Tensor ML terms). If no Android developer joins: none in the loop, and the slide states that llama.cpp CUDA is the only runtime that meets the 2 Hz perception loop on this Jetson; we do not claim the LiteRT award.

name: Reunite
one_liner: A lost-and-found concierge humanoid with on-device memory: EmbeddingGemma 2 indexes what the G1 has seen at its post, Gemma 4 E2B verifies and answers in the asker's language, and the robot turns, points, leads and waves to reunite a parent with a child or a traveller with their bottle, no faces stored, nothing leaving the robot.
story: A mall concourse on a Saturday. Our judge is a parent who looked at their phone for ten seconds and lost sight of a child. They run up to the humanoid standing at its post and say, in whatever language comes out first, 'Have you seen a boy in a red jacket?' The chest light turns cyan for a moment. 'Yes. About three minutes ago a child in a red jacket passed on my left, heading toward the café. I'll show you.' The robot turns toward where it saw him, raises its arm, and calls out; when the red jacket reappears at the edge of the crowd it waves and says 'There, on my right.' It does not walk the child anywhere; it keeps the parent and the child in sight and pulses red to call staff. Twenty minutes earlier the same robot told a traveller 'I saw a blue bottle placed on my tray by someone in a black hoodie four minutes ago; is this yours?' and handed it over. The presenter closes: this robot remembers like a good doorman, not like a surveillance camera. What it keeps is embeddings and twelve-word notes, in memory, wiped at the end of the shift; no faces, no cloud, no operator. One Gemma 4 E2B watched, listened and verified every answer; the two-week-old EmbeddingGemma 2 was its memory. When it has not seen something it says so, and here are its recall numbers on 40 queries, including the ones it got wrong.
demo_script: BENCH LOOP (about 6 min per group; robot in FSM 500 on a taped square at the end of the workbench facing the aisle, spotter on the remote, hip tray, chest webcam, log screen that shows the live memory feed: thumbnail, twelve-word note, time, heading). Seeding is continuous: a teammate in a bright green jacket wanders past the bench every few minutes; judges are invited to put a small item of theirs on the tray when they arrive. 0:00 Idle: white breathing LED; every 2 s a frame is noted ('man, black hoodie, blue bottle; woman, grey coat') and embedded; the log screen shows memory filling so judges see it is real. 0:30 PARTICIPATORY: the judge asks in their language 'Have you seen my colleague in the green jacket?' (XVF3800, lavalier or push-to-talk). Blue, then cyan; the audio tool returns find(description='person in green jacket', language=es); EmbeddingGemma 2 ranks the memory; E2B checks the top frames with 'Is a person in a green jacket in this image? yes/no'; the robot answers 'Yes, about two minutes ago, on my left, walking toward the exit' in the judge's language, turns toward that heading (yaw pulses), raises its arm (ExecuteAction 23). 1:15 Live watch: the 1 Hz question 'Is a person in a green jacket visible: left/center/right/no' runs; when the teammate reappears the robot waves (26) and says 'There, on my right.' 2:00 Lost item: the judge asks for the item they placed earlier; the robot recalls who placed it and when, confirms 'is this yours?', the tray trajectory lifts it, hand-detection yes, release. 3:00 VISIBLE FAILURE RECOVERY: a teammate asks for 'a man in a yellow hat' that never passed; the verifier returns no on every candidate; LED amber then red pulse; 'I haven't seen anyone like that in the last ten minutes. I'll alert staff and keep watching.' Honest negative, no invention. 3:45 Noisy repeat: with phone crowd noise the tool returns language=other or an empty description; 'This concourse is loud; who are you looking for, once more?' 4:30 The judge reads the memory screen and the numbers sheet; the presenter explains what is stored and the ten-minute wipe. STAGE (3 min): during setup the robot watches the stage edge for two minutes while a teammate in the red jacket crosses twice; live query from a volunteer judge; answer with time and side; turn, two Move pulses toward it, arm up, wave when the jacket reappears; one honest-negative query; red staff pulse; final slide with recall, verification and latency numbers; backup video ready.
gemma_role: Gemma 4 E2B (unsloth QAT UD-Q4_K_XL plus mmproj-BF16, llama-server CUDA arch 87, --jinja -ngl 99 -np 1 -c 4096 --swa-full --cache-ram 0, thinking off, greedy, cached prefix) does four jobs. (1) MEMORY NOTES while idle, 0.5 Hz: a chest-camera frame at 140 image tokens (clutter misses at 70) with 'List each visible person as clothing colour and what they carry, max 12 words' (max_tokens 24, about 1.3 s on the Orin), stored with the JPEG, timestamp and robot heading; paused during conversations so the fast path owns the GPU. (2) AUDIO INTENT: input_audio last, tools=[find(description: string, max 12 English words, language: enum[en, es, fr, de, zh, ja, ko, other])], max_tokens 40; a free-text argument plus one enum, within the two-argument reliability limit. (3) VERIFICATION: for the top-5 retrieved frames, 'Is there a <description> in this image? yes/no' (max_tokens 4, 0.3-0.45 s each); only verified hits are spoken, and no hit means an honest no. (4) LIVE WATCH after a hit: 'Is a <description> visible: left/center/right/no' at 1 Hz driving the turn and the wave. EmbeddingGemma 2 (740M, text plus image embeddings) supplies the retrieval; E2B supplies the words, the ears and the judgement. Why Gemma is essential: the memory is multimodal and multilingual by construction (a Spanish query embedded against English notes and raw frames), the verification step is vision question answering on arbitrary descriptions, which no detector offers, and the intent comes from native audio with no STT; the whole stack fits in 16 GB beside the robot services because E2B is small.
litert_role: Central and judge-visible: litert-lm serve runs EmbeddingGemma 2 on PC2 (CPU backend; /v1/embeddings since 0.18.0) as the robot's memory engine. Each memory entry stores an image embedding of the frame and a text embedding of the twelve-word note; a query is embedded as text and matched by cosine against both (numpy, under 1 ms for 300 entries). The index is a ten-minute ring buffer in RAM, wiped per shift. Expected costs: text embedding tens of ms (Pixel 11 Pro TPU does 8.3 ms; Orin CPU unmeasured), image embedding unknown on the Orin CPU (37 ms on an M5 Pro GPU; budget up to 1 s at 0.5 Hz; day-one spike), and if image embeddings are too slow the index becomes text-only over the E2B notes, still EmbeddingGemma 2 and still multilingual. LiteRT-LM GPU on the Orin is tried with the prebuilt linux_arm64 LD_LIBRARY_PATH workaround; whichever backend runs is named on the slide. Optional second surface if a teammate owns it: a Pi 5 'staff pager' display is deliberately not built, because padding hurts; the LiteRT claim rests on the memory engine alone.
architecture: PC2 processes: llama-server (E2B, :8080); litert-lm serve (EmbeddingGemma 2, :9379); watcher.py (chest USB webcam with a wide field of view, since the D435i view is fixed with no head joints; 480x336 JPEG q85 at 140 image tokens for memory frames, 70 for live-watch questions; frames to tmpfs); memory.py (ring buffer of {t, heading_yaw from rt/odommodestate, jpeg path, note, img_vec, txt_vec}, 10 min retention, cosine search, verification queue, shift wipe); ears.py (ReSpeaker XVF3800 at 16 kHz, energy VAD, 8 s cap, DOA azimuth, lavalier and chest push-to-talk alternatives); conductor.py (IDLE/WATCH -> LISTEN -> FIND -> VERIFY -> ANSWER -> LEAD -> SPOT -> STAFF_ALERT; LED: white idle, blue listening, cyan searching, green verified hit, amber unsure, red pulse staff alert; the LEAD state is at most two Move(0.3,0,0) pulses with the lidar sector guard from rt/utlidar/cloud_livox_mid and never toward a child, only toward the parent's side); voice.py (Piper, multilingual answer templates filled with time-ago, side and the note; free text only for the note itself); body.py (LocoClient FSM 500 yaw pulses, ExecuteAction 23/26/27/99, rt/arm_sdk tray trajectory with the arm service toggled, rt/brainco/right/cmd and /state). name: Show Once (one-shot chore imitation from the robot's own eyes)
one_liner: A person performs a 2-3 step tabletop chore in front of the G1 once; Gemma 4 E2B turns the robot's own video into a named, grounded recipe (objects, order, zones, gesture), says it back, and the robot repeats it, including a judge's on-the-spot variation.
story: Every home has a hundred tiny chores that nobody will ever write a program for: put the cup back on the tray, move the can to the shelf, wave goodbye. You should not have to program them. You should be able to show them once. This is a Unitree G1 with two five-finger hands, and inside it is a single Gemma 4 E2B model running on the robot's own Jetson, no network, nothing to phone home to. Watch: I take the red cup, put it on the yellow tray, and wave. (10 seconds.) The robot watched its own camera. It picked the frames where my hand stopped moving, asked itself what my hand was holding and where things ended up, and wrote this recipe: pick red cup from slot B, place on left tray, wave. It says it back in my words. Now it does it. Here is the honest part, on the screen: what it LEARNED is the recipe, from one viewing. What we BUILT are the verbs: pick-from-slot, place-in-zone, point, wave, hand over. It cannot learn a new verb by watching, and we are not claiming it can. Now you try: change the object, the tray or the gesture, and it will repeat yours. And when a step fails, the robot checks with its own eyes and tries again or asks for help, which is what a disciplined embodied system should do.
demo_script: BENCH (loop runs continuously; judges rotate past; whole cycle 90 s; PTT button on the table). 0:00 Robot standing docked at a 75 cm table with a printed placemat (slots A/B/C, LEFT TRAY, RIGHT TRAY), chest webcam looking at the mat, 'mind' screen beside it showing live camera, 'NO DEFAULT ROUTE / robot AP only' badge, last keyframes, Gemma answers with ms, recipe with provenance tags, autonomous success counter from rehearsals. 0:10 Presenter: 'Watch me once' and performs: pick blue can from slot A, place on right tray, high-five gesture (8-12 s). LED amber = watching. 0:25 Screen shows 4-5 keyframes popping out at wrist-speed minima (MoveNet on LiteRT), each annotated by Gemma: boxes for can/cup/tray/hand and the one-word hand state (holding/empty/waving). 0:35 Robot (Piper voice): 'You moved the blue can from slot A to the right tray, then gave a high five. I will do that now.' Recipe appears as JSON with tags [learned] and [verb: XR-recorded 10/21]. 0:40 Robot executes: arm_sdk trajectory to slot A, BrainCo close to 0.7, lift, place on right tray, open, then ExecuteAction(18) high five toward the judge. Each step gated by a vision check ('Is the can on the right tray? yes/no', ~1 s). 1:15 PARTICIPATORY: judge is asked to show a variant (any of 3 objects, either tray, wave or heart). Robot narrates the judge's version back ('red cup to the left tray, then a heart') and repeats it. Judge may say 'again' / 'otra vez' / '再来一次' into the lavalier; Gemma audio-in maps it to repeat(). 1:50 FAILURE-RECOVERY (staged once per round or natural): teammate nudges the cup off the tray during placement, or the grasp slips. Post-step check fails; LED red; robot says 'The cup is not on the tray. Let me try again' and re-runs place from the known slot; if the object left the mat it says 'Please put the cup back on slot B' and waits for the vision check to pass. 2:10 Presenter points at the counter: 'N autonomous runs this week, X% complete, median perception answer Y ms on the Jetson' and the provenance panel. STAGE (2.5 min): 0:00 story opener (above) 0:30 presenter demonstrates the chore 0:45 keyframes and recipe projected 1:00 robot executes 1:40 a volunteer from the audience shows a variant (object + tray + gesture) 2:10 recovery moment (vision check catches a misplaced item) 2:25 numbers slide, 'everything on the robot, no network', backup video ready on the laptop.
gemma_role: One model: Gemma 4 E2B (unsloth gemma-4-E2B-it-qat UD-Q4_K_XL + mmproj, the audio encoder is inside the mmproj) on llama-server built with CUDA arch 87 on PC2, flags from run_llama.sh plus -np 1 --cache-ram 0 -c 4096 --swa-full --jinja, thinking off, greedy. Calls: (1) per keyframe, image first then the question: 'detect can, cup, tray, hand' with assistant prefill of the JSON list, box_2d on the 0-1000 grid, 672x480 frame = 140 image tokens (70 misses objects in clutter per Google's own doc), ~17 output tokens per object, stop on ']'; (2) per keyframe one-word hand state ('Is the hand holding something, empty, pointing, or waving? one word', 1-2 tokens); (3) one text-only call that names the chore and composes the spoken summary from the code-derived step list (<=40 output tokens; text-only percept->plan mapping is the one composition E2B did reliably in the harness); (4) audio-native commands: 5-10 s 16 kHz mono clip placed after the text, tools repeat(), skip_step(step), stop(), set_language(lang), each <=2 args validated client-side; (5) execution verification: yes/no questions after every step ('Is the blue can on the right tray?'). Why Gemma is essential: the same model grounds objects, reads hand semantics, names and narrates the chore, understands spoken variations in any language, and verifies outcomes; replacing it would need a detector, an ASR, an LLM and a VQA model, and still lack 'what is the hand doing'. Sequencing, geometry and safety are code (state machine), presented as the point: Gemma perceives and decides at every branch; code enforces the envelope.
litert_role: Genuinely in the loop twice, both CPU-reliable: (1) keyframe selection runs MoveNet Lightning (int8 .tflite, 192x192, wrist keypoints) through ai-edge-litert 2.3.0's Interpreter (manylinux aarch64 wheel, XNNPACK) at ~15-30 fps on the Orin CPU; wrist-speed minima pick the 3-6 keyframes Gemma looks at (SeeDo's recipe, which was the difference between 60% and ~0% in their paper); (2) chore memory: EmbeddingGemma 2 (embeddinggemma-2-740m-litert-lm, 485 MB) served by litert-lm serve on port 9379, /v1/embeddings; each learned chore is stored as text+keyframe embeddings and a spoken request ('do the tray thing from yesterday') is embedded as audio/text and matched by cosine similarity before Gemma 4 confirms. Day-one bonus: if LiteRT-LM 0.18 GPU runs on PC2 with the prebuilt/linux_arm64 LD_LIBRARY_PATH workaround, route the one non-latency-critical naming call through it so two Gemma engines are visibly on the slide. The sub-second perception loop stays on llama.cpp CUDA and we say so.
architecture: Devices: only PC2 (Orin NX 16 GB, JetPack 6.2) runs compute; a laptop/tablet shows the 'mind' web page served by PC2 over the robot's own MT7612U AP (display only). Sensors: chest-mounted USB webcam (Logitech C920, 640x480 at 30 fps via OpenCV V4L2) looking down at the mat, because the G1 has no head joints and the fixed D435i looks over a close table; D435i RGB via V4L2 as a second view for the stage. Audio: ReSpeaker XVF3800 USB array on the chest (AEC, beamforming, DOA) or a UAC wireless lavalier on the presenter/judge, push-to-talk via a USB HID arcade button (or an unbound key on rt/wirelesscontroller held by the spotter); Silero VAD chunks <=10 s. Pipeline: webcam -> MoveNet (LiteRT, CPU) -> wrist speed -> keyframes -> llama-server (Gemma 4 E2B, GPU) box_2d + hand-state per keyframe -> code diff of object states between keyframes -> recipe JSON -> Gemma names/narrates -> Piper TTS (aarch64 binary) -> USB speaker (ALSA) with AudioClient.PlayStream(16 kHz mono int16, 50 ms chunks) as fallback; LEDs via AudioClient.LedControl (>=200 ms apart: amber watching, blue listening, green understood, red recovery). angle: Learn-from-watching and embodied intelligence, done honestly. The event text asks for "a robot that learns a chore from watching you once" and "sees, hears, reasons and acts"; the Gemma judges reward "disciplined, non-hallucinatory design", auditable reasoning, offline operation and real numbers, and the AGI House robotics crowd discounts teleop. So every concept here separates what is LEARNED in one viewing (the recipe: which objects, which order, which zones, which names, which places) from what is PRE-BUILT (the verbs: parameterized skills with provenance labels: canned Unitree gesture / XR-guided recording / parametric code), shows both on a "robot's mind" screen next to measured latencies, logs an autonomous success-rate table, and keeps the XR headset in a closed box at demo time. The three concepts are three different learning modes with different risk profiles: (1) Show Once = procedure imitation from the robot's own camera (arms, tabletop); (2) Apprentice = motor skills taught by guiding the robot's hands once via the existing XR teleop, labeled by Gemma from the robot's own video and recalled by voice in any language, with a live teaching moment at the bench (arms, lowest risk because teleop already works on this robot); (3) Show Me Around = a guided tour that becomes a spoken-place map, then one-sentence errands that the robot walks, verifies and reports (legs, continuity with the fetch-a-drink navigation leg). All three share one stack on PC2 (llama.cpp CUDA for Gemma 4 E2B reflexes; LiteRT for MoveNet keyframing and LiteRT-LM for EmbeddingGemma 2 memory; Piper TTS; a USB mic with push-to-talk), so the team can start one and fall back to another without re-platforming. The crucial first-48-hour facts are the same for all three: does Gemma audio run on the Orin under llama.cpp CUDA, does rt/arm_sdk replay hold balance in FSM 500, does LocoClient move on this firmware, and does a USB mic give usable speech in a loud room.

name: Apprentice (guide its hands once, then just say the word)
one_liner: A human guides the G1's arms and five-finger hands through a new move once with the existing XR teleop; Gemma 4 E2B watches the robot's own camera, names the skill and its preconditions, stores it, and from then on anyone can trigger it by voice in any language, with the headset in a box and no operator at demo time.
story: For ten thousand years this is how humans taught hands: the master guides the apprentice's hands through the motion once, then just says the name of the move. We built that for a humanoid. Yesterday I put on a headset and guided this robot's arms through a handover and a table wipe, once each. It watched itself through its own camera, and Gemma 4, running on the Jetson inside its chest, named what it had just done and wrote down what has to be true before it can do it again: 'a can on the mat'. Today the headset is in that box. Everything you see now is the robot listening and deciding on its own: you can speak English, Spanish or Mandarin, the sound goes straight into Gemma, no speech-to-text in between, and it answers with a tool call that picks the skill and checks the scene first. Here is the honest line, on the screen: the MOTIONS were taught by guidance, like a coach moving a student's arm, and they are replayed, not improvised; the UNDERSTANDING is learned: the name, the precondition, the language, the choice. And now the part I like best: give me a move you want it to learn, right now, and we will teach it in front of you in sixty seconds.
demo_script: BENCH (judges rotate; a cycle is 60-90 s; two taught skills always ready: hand-over-the-can and wipe-the-mat; a library of 8-12 skills on the screen with provenance 'taught by XR guidance on 10/21, take 1, 6.2 s'). 0:00 Screen: library, live chest camera, 'NO DEFAULT ROUTE' badge, headset visibly in a closed box labeled 'teaching tool, not used during demo'. 0:10 Judge takes the PTT button and the lavalier and asks for anything in their language ('dame la lata' / 'hand me the can' / '把罐子给我'). Blue LED while the 6 s clip goes to Gemma. 0:12 Within ~2 s the mind screen shows the tool call: do_skill(name='hand_over_can', lang='es') plus the audio token count and ms. 0:14 Precondition check: Gemma yes/no on the current frame ('Is there a can on the mat? yes'). 0:16 Replay: rt/arm_sdk trajectory reaches slot B, BrainCo closes to 0.7, lifts, extends toward the judge; the robot says 'Aquí tienes' (Piper es voice); release gated by a vision question at 2 Hz ('Is a human hand holding the can?') with a spoken prompt after 4 s. 0:40 PARTICIPATORY/LIVE LEARNING: judge names a new move ('a salute', 'knock twice on the table', 'thumbs up'); teammate puts on the Quest, presses r then s, guides the move for ~5 s, presses s; headset goes back in the box. Screen shows the recording's keyframes (MoveNet wrist minima) and Gemma's label and precondition ('right hand raised to the forehead: salute; no object needed'). 1:10 Judge triggers it by voice; robot performs the salute and greets them in their language. 1:30 FAILURE-RECOVERY (natural or staged): judge asks for the hand-over with the can removed from the mat; precondition fails; LED red; robot: 'I don't see a can on the mat. Please put it on slot B'; the judge places it; the check passes and the skill runs. Second recovery type: a noisy clip yields a low-confidence/unknown skill; the robot repeats what it understood ('You want the salute, right?') and waits for yes/no audio. 1:50 Presenter: autonomous success table from the week (per skill, n and successes), audio-to-tool-call median ms on the Jetson, 'E2B hears 8 languages natively; we verified these three'. STAGE (2.5 min): 0:00 apprenticeship opener 0:30 a volunteer invents a move; teammate teaches it live (45 s including labeling) 1:20 volunteer triggers it by voice in their own language 1:40 hand-over of a can to the volunteer with the vision-gated release 2:05 the 'no can on the mat' recovery 2:25 numbers and the headset-in-the-box line; backup video ready.
gemma_role: Gemma 4 E2B (same cached unsloth QAT GGUF + mmproj) on llama-server CUDA on PC2, thinking off, greedy. (1) Voice to action with no ASR stage: a VAD-chunked 16 kHz mono clip of <=10 s is placed after a short text prompt ('Pick the skill the person asked for and reply in their language'), and the model emits do_skill(name, lang) or ask(question) via native tool calls; the skill enum is validated client-side because the native tool grammar does not enforce enums; the library names are listed in the cached system prefix (<=200 tokens). (2) Skill labeling at teach time: 3-5 keyframes from the recording (chest camera, 480x336 = 70 tokens each, or 140 if the mat is cluttered) each get a direct question ('What is the robot's right hand doing? one phrase' and 'What object is in the hand? one word'); then a text-only call composes name + precondition ('a can on the mat' / 'none') and the spoken confirmation. Optional one-time thinking with a 128-token budget here since it is not latency-critical. (3) Pre/post-condition checks: yes/no questions on the live frame (1-2 output tokens) and the handover release gate ('Is a human hand holding the can?'). (4) Multilingual replies: Gemma writes the sentence in the detected language; Piper speaks it (es/zh/fr/de voices preloaded). Why Gemma is essential: native audio understanding plus tool calling plus vision checks plus language detection in one 5 GB model; the memory-routing story the judges praised (one model, no Whisper, thinking off for latency) is built in. Honesty line: Gemma does not generate motion; the controller replays taught joint trajectories inside a code-enforced envelope.
litert_role: Two visible jobs on CPU: (1) skill memory: EmbeddingGemma 2 via litert-lm serve /v1/embeddings embeds each skill's label text and keyframe images; a spoken request is embedded (audio part, or the transcript Gemma returns) and the top-3 cosine matches are passed to Gemma 4 as the candidate enum, which keeps the tool-call prompt short as the library grows and gives judges a second Gemma-family model to point at; (2) MoveNet Lightning through ai-edge-litert's Interpreter selects keyframes of the teaching clip (same code as Show Once). Conditional: if the day-one LiteRT-LM GPU test on PC2 passes (prebuilt/linux_arm64 LD_LIBRARY_PATH workaround), the teach-time labeling call runs on LiteRT-LM so the slide shows LiteRT-LM running Gemma 4 on the robot; otherwise we say plainly that the Gemma inference is llama.cpp CUDA and LiteRT-LM serves embeddings.
architecture: Teach time (home, Oct 19-22, and live at the bench): Quest 3 on the robot's own AP (10.42.0.1), xr_teleoperate teleop_hand_and_arm.py --input-mode controller --arm G1_23 --ee brainco --network-interface eth0 --record --task-name <skill>, r to start tracking, s to start/stop; EpisodeWriter writes episode_XXXX/data.json with states/actions qpos per arm (5 joints per arm on the 23-DoF body) and 6 BrainCo values per hand at 30 Hz plus colors; a converter trims idle head/tail, resamples to 50 Hz, clips joint velocity and stores skill.json {name, precondition, trajectory, hand, duration, provenance}. Demo time, all on PC2 over DDS eth0: PTT/VAD -> clip -> llama-server (audio) -> tool call -> state machine -> precondition vision check (chest webcam V4L2 640x480; D435i RGB via V4L2 as the stage view) -> replay publisher: hg LowCmd on rt/arm_sdk at 50 Hz through G1_23_ArmController (kp 80/kd 3, wrist 40/1.5, weight ramp on joint 29 over 1 s, 2 s blend from the current pose to the first recorded pose, replay at 0.7x speed, abort on IMU tilt or joint error > threshold, ctrl_dual_arm_go_home at the end), hands on rt/brainco/{left,right}/cmd; prerequisite RobotStateClient.ServiceSwitch('g1_arm_example', 0) and FSM 500 (R1+X) or locked stand (L2+Up); alternative replay path to test day one: if the Unitree app's teach function exists on this firmware, G1ArmActionClient.ExecuteAction(name) replays taught actions under Unitree's own balance controller (non-blocking, StopCustomAction to abort), which would be the lowest-risk path. Speech out: Gemma text -> Piper (aarch64 binary) -> USB speaker via ALSA, PlayStream fallback; LEDs via LedControl. DOA from the XVF3800 (xvf_host AEC_AZIMUTH) turns the robot toward the speaker with a LocoClient.Move yaw pulse when locomotion works. Expected latencies (projections, measure day 1): audio clip 6 s = 150 audio tokens + encoder, tool call ~13 tokens: 1.5-2.5 s on the Orin; precondition check 0.6-1.0 s; replay 5-10 s; labeling at teach time 5-8 s for 4 keyframes. Memory: E2B server ~5 GB GPU, EmbeddingGemma 2 ~1 GB CPU, Piper 0.2 GB; the teleop stack (pinocchio IK) only during teaching. No cloud: the headset page is self-signed https on the robot AP; no default route on PC2.
